groups.sentence: Instructors collect an in-person or handwritten baseline writing sample from students early in the course.
Instructors may use rubric descriptors or tags to mark repetitive or generic writing while grading.
Instructors compare suspicious work with the student's earlier or in-class writing to spot changes in style or quality.
Writing style or quality that differs from the student's previous work or the class can signal AI use.
Instructors review submitted work for unusual, inconsistent or suspicious features when they suspect AI use.
Instructors check that cited sources exist and are accurate, since AI often fabricates citations.
Fabricated or nonexistent citations and references can signal AI-written work.
Instructors document concrete evidence before pursuing an AI misconduct case, and may report suspicions based on style or invented sources.
Instructors may run their assignment prompt through an AI tool and compare the output with student work.
Content beyond or outside the course material or assignment requirements can signal AI use.
A student's inability to explain or defend their submitted work can signal AI use.
These signs are not certain proof of AI use.
